newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Confusion over state of Colombian truck strike.
newsitem.headline: Confusion over state of Colombian truck strike.

text.p: Confusion surrounded Colombia's crippling week-old trucking strike on Sunday as union leaders said it was holding firm while government officials said it had collapsed after declaring it illegal.

Javier Suarez, chairman of the Colombian Truck Drivers Association, said 90 percent of road cargo, including key coal and coffee exports, remained paralyzed despite government efforts to undermine the strike with weekend offers of a partial solution.
But Transport Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez said most truckers were returning to work and he threatened sanctions against those who did not.

"The reports I have from across the country are that the situation continues exactly the same and truckers will not move again until their basic demands have been met," Suarez said in a telephone interview. "Undoubtedly this strike implies a great sacrifice on the part of our members but truck driving is just not profitable these days."

Late on Friday the government ruled the strike was illegal. In a detailed press statement on Saturday, Hernan Lopez said a series of offers had been put to the truckers and any still on strike by Sunday risked having their operators' licenses revoked.
Suarez said on Sunday that he believed 80 or 90 percent of the truck drivers' association members were going back to work after the week-long stoppage.

The independent association's basic demands include a 30 percent raise in freight rates, which it says should be set by the government and not by private transportation companies as it is now. It also wants private transportation firms to lift what it says is a "unilateral veto" on contracting trucks more than 10 years old.

The partial solution offered by the Transport Ministry on Saturday allowed for a 15 percent increase in cargo rates and for drivers to increase their vehicles' load-bearing capacity providing the trucks were professionally modified.

Suarez explained: "We're holding out for a 30 percent raise in rates because at present the intermediaries, the transport companies, hold on to as much as 60 percent of the charge. Our stoppage may be affecting industry and agriculture, but truck drivers cannot continue subsidizing other sectors of the economy."

He said he expected talks to resume with government officials on Monday, adding that he was calling for direct negotiations with Interior Minister Horacio Serpa in the face of what he described as Hernan Lopez's unwillingness to solve the dispute.
